items.stem: The Albany Plan of Union failed because
options: the plan required the northeastern colonies to contribute a disproportionate share of the necessary troops and money
no political leader with national stature was willing to support the plan
there was no legitimate executive power to enforce it
none of the colonies was willing to share tax-collecting powers with a national entity
items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin developed the Albany Plan, a first stab at a united colonial government empowered to collect taxes and raise a military. Although the delegations to Albany signed off on the plan, none of the colonial legislatures would have anything to do with it; they were uninterested in ceding any powers, even in the interest of strengthening the colonies as a whole. Around the same time, Franklin’s famous “Join or Die” cartoon showed the colonies as a snake cut into segments, each representing a colony.

option_explanations.A: The plan did not single out the northeastern colonies for disproportionate contributions. Colonial legislatures rejected the plan outright rather than quarreling over shares of troops and money.
option_explanations.B: A leader of national stature did back the plan — Benjamin Franklin authored it and promoted it with his 'Join or Die' cartoon. Lack of a champion was not the problem.
option_explanations.C: The Albany Plan actually proposed an executive (a president-general) alongside a grand council. The failure was not a missing executive but the colonies' refusal to give up any of their own powers.
option_explanations.D: The delegations at Albany approved Franklin's plan, but not one colonial legislature would ratify it. Each colony refused to surrender tax-collecting power to a continental body, even for common defense during the French and Indian War.

items.stem: The American colonists objected to the policies imposed by Parliament after the French and Indian War for all of the following reasons EXCEPT
options: the new restrictions would hinder New England trade
their rights as Englishmen were being violated
they resented quartering British troops now that the French threat was removed
they wanted colonial representatives seated in Parliament in London
items.explanation: 1763, the year the Treaty of Paris ended the French and Indian War, is often considered to be a major turning point in British-colonial relations as it marked the end of Britain’s policy of salutary neglect. Beginning with the Proclamation of 1763, the colonists began to feel England tightening the screws. The passage of the Sugar and Stamp Acts set off a chain of new restrictions that set the colonists on the road to revolution. Although you no doubt know the phrase “No taxation without representation,” the colonists did not actually want to send colonial representatives to sit in the British Parliament in London. Rather, they believed that only their own colonial legislatures had the power to tax them, as shown through resolutions adopted by the Stamp Act Congress. They initially understood that they were British subjects and that Parliament had the right to enact mercantilist restrictions to regulate trade. However, they soon voiced their concern that there was a significant difference between taxation and legislation.

option_explanations.A: New England merchants did object that measures like the Sugar Act hindered their trade, so this was a genuine colonial grievance, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Colonists genuinely argued that Parliament was violating their rights as Englishmen — above all the right not to be taxed without consent — so this was a real objection, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Colonists genuinely resented having to house and supply British troops once the French threat was gone, so this was a real objection, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: 'No taxation without representation' did not mean colonists wanted seats in Parliament. They wanted taxation only by their own colonial assemblies; sending a few delegates to London was never their demand, so this is the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the Boston Massacre is true?
options: Several of the soldiers involved were imprisoned without trial, which increased British animosity toward the colonists.
The shootings were essentially unprovoked, which increased American animosity toward the British.
The Quartering Act of 1765 was largely responsible for the underlying tensions that ultimately led to violence.
The incident led to immediate calls for war by most political leaders on both sides of the conflict.
items.explanation: The Boston Massacre of 1770 was largely the result of simmering tensions among the colonists regarding the Quartering Act of 1765, which required civilians to house British soldiers. Bostonians formed an angry mob, and some threw rocks at soldiers, who responded by shooting several of the rioters. Despite the ensuing outrage in the colonies, the accused soldiers were given a fair trial at which they were represented by John Adams. Leaders on both sides toned down their rhetoric after the shocking incident for fear matters would escalate.

option_explanations.A: The soldiers were not imprisoned without trial. They received a fair trial in which John Adams himself served as their defense counsel; most were acquitted and two were convicted of manslaughter.
option_explanations.B: The shootings were not unprovoked. An angry Boston mob surrounded the soldiers and threw rocks and ice at them before the soldiers fired.
option_explanations.C: The Quartering Act of 1765 required colonists to house British soldiers, and the presence of redcoats in Boston bred years of resentment. Those underlying tensions exploded into violence in the 1770 Massacre.
option_explanations.D: Leaders on both sides deliberately cooled their rhetoric after the shootings for fear of escalation. There were no immediate calls for war from most political leaders on either side.

items.stem: The Stamp Act Congress of 1765 was historically significant in that it
options: represented a first step in colonial unity against Britain
demonstrated Parliament’s determination to tax its American colonies
represented New England’s determination to go to war against England
demonstrated the colonists’ political and philosophical disagreement among themselves
items.explanation: The Stamp Act Congress was a gathering of representatives from several colonies to address the newly enacted Stamp Act. This represented the first (of several) Continental Congress meetings to address British taxation practices. The Stamp Act Congress of 1765 is historically significant because it marked the beginning of colonial unity and resistance against the British, so (A) is the correct answer. Eliminate (B), as the Stamp Act of 1765 was a reaction to the Parliament’s determination to tax the American Colonies without representation. One could argue that most colonists still considered themselves to be loyal British subjects even after fighting had begun in Lexington and Concord in April 1775, so eliminate (C) as well. Finally, (D) most likely refers to the Albany Plan of Union, proposed by Benjamin Franklin at the start of the French and Indian War, which was rejected by colonists in favor of maintaining individual colonial sovereignty.

option_explanations.A: Nine colonies sent delegates to New York in 1765 to coordinate petitions and boycotts against the Stamp Act — the first joint political action by the colonies against Britain, and the start of intercolonial unity.
option_explanations.B: The Stamp Act itself demonstrated Parliament's determination to tax the colonies. The Congress demonstrated the opposite: colonial resistance, not Parliament's will.
option_explanations.C: In 1765 New England was not determined to go to war; most colonists still considered themselves loyal British subjects. War was still a decade away.
option_explanations.D: The Congress produced unified petitions and a coordinated boycott — a show of agreement across colonies, not of philosophical disagreement.

items.stem: Thomas Jefferson relied on the ideas of John Locke in writing the American Declaration of Independence in all of the following ways EXCEPT Locke’s belief that
options: man is born free and equal
man must submit to the General Will
governments get their authority from the people, not God
the purpose of government is to protect man’s natural rights
items.explanation: Much of the American Declaration of Independence is derived from the writings of John Locke, particularly his Two Treatises of Government, published in 1690, in which he challenged the theory of divine right of kings and put forth what is known as social contract theory. Both Locke and Rousseau believed that man was born free, but it was Rousseau who argued that “Man must be forced to be free” and submit to the “General Will.”

option_explanations.A: Locke did argue that men are born free and equal in the state of nature — a premise Jefferson echoes in 'all men are created equal.'
option_explanations.B: The 'General Will' — and the idea that man must be 'forced to be free' — comes from Rousseau's Social Contract (1762), not from Locke. This is the belief Jefferson did not take from Locke.
option_explanations.C: Locke's social contract theory holds that governments derive authority from the consent of the governed, directly challenging the divine right of kings — a foundation of the Declaration.
option_explanations.D: Locke argued that government's purpose is to protect natural rights (life, liberty, and property) — the direct model for the Declaration's 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.'

items.stem: Historians often cite Shays’s Rebellion (1786–1787) as a significant event in U.S. history because it
options: demonstrated the strength, yet fairness, of the newly created federal government
made many Americans realize that slavery could not last
made Americans realize that excessive taxation often leads to violence
demonstrated the weakness of the federal government under the Articles of Confederation
items.explanation: The Articles of Confederation had intentionally created a weak central government, granting Congress few regulatory powers to avoid creating an American Parliament. Shays’s Rebellion threatened the survival of the newly established republic because farmers in western Massachusetts were rebelling against their state government for the very same reason colonists had rebelled against England—taxes. Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could neither raise nor support a federal militia, so when Massachusetts requested federal assistance in squelching Daniel Shays and his farmer friends, no help was available. Had this question been about the Whiskey Rebellion during George Washington’s administration, (A) would have been the correct answer. Choice (A) also demonstrates the difference between the limited power of the federal government under the Articles of Confederation and the stronger federal government established by the Constitution. Choice (C) is not correct, although excessive taxation was certainly one of the major causes of the American Revolution and subsequent rebellions. It is interesting to note that we did not have a federal income tax until the Sixteenth Amendment was ratified in the early 20th century.

option_explanations.A: Shays's Rebellion exposed weakness, not strength. It happened in 1786-87, under the Articles of Confederation — the new federal government under the Constitution did not yet exist.
option_explanations.B: Slavery was not at issue in Shays's Rebellion. Massachusetts farmers rose against state taxes and debt foreclosures, not over slavery.
option_explanations.C: Excessive taxation did anger the farmers, but historians cite the rebellion's significance differently: it proved the national government under the Articles was too weak to keep order, which pushed leaders toward the Constitutional Convention.
option_explanations.D: Congress under the Articles could neither levy taxes nor raise a federal force, so Massachusetts had to suppress Daniel Shays's uprising on its own. The episode demonstrated the Articles' weakness and helped trigger the 1787 Constitutional Convention.

items.stem: Under the Articles of Confederation, the national government had which of the following powers? The power to collect taxes The power to negotiate treaties The power to supersede state law
options: I only
II only
I and III only
I, II, and III
items.explanation: The Articles of Confederation were established to provide a limited framework to organize the states under a single banner. However, they had very little power (purposefully) so that each state could create its own government and legislation. States were expected to establish taxation, while Congress was not authorized to enact taxes under the Articles of Confederation (eliminating I). Furthermore, the whole purpose of the Articles of Confederation was to provide a legal document to enforce states’ rights, not undermine them (eliminating III). The Articles of Confederation did, however, provide a framework for how the United States government would represent the states in foreign diplomatic matters such as treaties (making II correct).

option_explanations.A: Incorrect — tax collection was power I, which Congress did not have. Under the Articles, Congress could only request money from the states, not levy taxes.
option_explanations.B: Correct — treaty negotiation was power II, which Congress did have (it negotiated the 1783 Treaty of Paris ending the Revolution). Powers I (taxes) and III (overriding state law) were deliberately withheld.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect — it pairs power I (taxes), which Congress lacked, with power III (superseding state law), which the Articles never granted. The whole point of the Articles was to protect state sovereignty.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect — Congress had only power II. It could not tax (I) and it could not override state law (III); there was no supremacy clause under the Articles.

items.stem: George Washington established the principle of executive privilege in a dispute with Congress over the
options: Alien and Sedition Acts
legality of political parties
Jay Treaty
Whiskey Rebellion
items.explanation: Washington’s presidency was all about establishing precedents. He was extremely conscious of this fact and proceeded cautiously throughout his two terms, aware that future presidents would follow his example. Thus, he rarely used his presidential veto, hoping to encourage future executives to accommodate the legislature on most matters. He didn’t want Congress to have complete control over the executive branch, though, and believed in the system of checks and balances. Thus, when the House of Representatives demanded all of Washington’s papers regarding negotiations for the unpopular Jay Treaty, Washington refused. He reasoned that the papers were none of the House’s business because only the Senate—with whom Washington did share the papers—is required to ratify treaties. His action established the precedent of executive privilege, a nebulous executive right to protect sensitive information and executive privacy. The right is occasionally invoked by presidents and frequently challenged by Congress, with the two typically working out a compromise before the matter can reach the courts.

option_explanations.A: The Alien and Sedition Acts were passed in 1798 under President John Adams, after Washington had left office — the wrong president and the wrong dispute.
option_explanations.B: Washington warned against political parties in his Farewell Address, but the executive-privilege precedent came from his refusal to hand over diplomatic papers, not from a dispute about parties.
option_explanations.C: When the House demanded all of Washington's papers on the negotiations behind the unpopular Jay Treaty (1795), he refused — establishing the precedent that presidents may withhold executive-branch communications from Congress.
option_explanations.D: The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) established a different precedent: Washington's use of federal troops showed the new government would enforce its laws. It was not about withholding documents from Congress.

items.stem: The proponents of The Virginia Plan would have supported which of the following in forming the body of the U.S. Constitution?
options: Adoption of the Articles of Confederation with minor modifications
Equal state representation in legislature regardless of population size
A unicameral legislative body
Three separate branches of government
items.explanation: In drafting the U.S. Constitution, supporters of the New Jersey plan advocated a tweaked or modified form of the Articles of Confederation with a unicameral (single-bodied) legislature in which the states would have equal representation in legislative decisions. In contrast, the Virginia Plan advocated for a new system of government with three branches including a bicameral (two-bodied) legislature with representation based on population size. While the Virginia Plan ultimately became the basis for the U.S. Constitution, the equal representation of the states regardless of population remains the rule of governance for the U.S. Senate.

option_explanations.A: Adopting the Articles with minor modifications was the New Jersey Plan's position, the rival of the Virginia Plan.
option_explanations.B: Equal representation for every state regardless of population was the New Jersey Plan's core demand. The Virginia Plan called for representation based on population.
option_explanations.C: A single-chamber legislature was the system under the Articles and the New Jersey Plan. The Virginia Plan proposed a bicameral legislature.
option_explanations.D: The Virginia Plan called for an entirely new government with three separate branches — legislative, executive, and judicial — and a two-house legislature apportioned by population.

items.stem: Which of the following best fits the profile of a Democratic-Republican?
options: A wealthy merchant from New York who desires a strict interpretation of the Constitution
A zealous supporter of the National Bank
A yeoman farmer from South Carolina whose sympathies lie with France
An advocate for centralized power and a strong alliance with England
items.explanation: Democratic-Republicans, who favored state power and a strict interpretation of the Constitution, tended to be southern yeoman farmers who desired an economy based on agriculture and a strong alliance with France. They viewed the establishment of a National Bank as desirable but not critical. In contrast, the federalists, who favored a powerful central government and a loose interpretation of the Constitution, tended to be wealthy northeasterners who desired an economy based on commerce and a close alliance with England. They wholeheartedly approved of a National Bank, which they deemed essential to successful governance.

option_explanations.A: This profile is internally contradictory: wealthy merchants backed the Federalists, who favored a loose (not strict) interpretation of the Constitution and a strong central government.
option_explanations.B: Zealous support for the National Bank was the Federalist (Hamiltonian) position. Democratic-Republicans were skeptical of the Bank as an overreach of federal power.
option_explanations.C: Democratic-Republicans were Jefferson's party: southern and western yeoman farmers who favored agriculture, states' rights, strict construction of the Constitution, and sympathy with revolutionary France against Britain.
option_explanations.D: Centralized power and a close alliance with England describe the Federalists, the Democratic-Republicans' opponents.

items.stem: All of the following were immediate social or economic consequences of the American Revolution EXCEPT
options: increased opportunities for land settlement in the West
reform of primogeniture inheritance laws
expanded rights for women to hold property
the opening of many areas of trade and manufacture
items.explanation: First, cross out “EXCEPT” from the question and determine whether each answer is true or false based on the question stem. The American Revolution Era in the late 1700s was when the colonies broke from Great Britain, and the main disputes were taxing and trading laws. Most people lived on the Atlantic coast. Choices (A) and (D) are firmly within the American Revolution, so they’re both true. Remember that this is an EXCEPT question, so if an answer choice is true, eliminate it! Maybe you’re not sure between (B) and (C), so which of these things is least like the others? That would be (C), expanded rights for women to hold property. Women’s rights did not become an issue until decades later, in the mid-1800s, with the Seneca Falls convention and the first women’s rights movement. Choice (C) is then false, which makes it the correct answer for this EXCEPT question.

option_explanations.A: Western land settlement did expand as an immediate consequence of independence — the end of British restrictions and then the Northwest Ordinance (1787) opened new opportunities.
option_explanations.B: Several states did reform inheritance law right after independence, abolishing primogeniture and entail (Virginia did so in 1776) — a genuine immediate consequence.
option_explanations.C: Women's property rights did not expand after the Revolution. Under coverture, married women's legal identity remained subsumed in their husbands', and women's legal status was essentially unchanged.
option_explanations.D: Independence ended the Navigation Acts, opening American merchants and manufacturers to new markets — a genuine immediate economic consequence.
